newsitem.title: USA: U.S. bomb trial jurors want to ask McVeigh Why?.
newsitem.headline: U.S. bomb trial jurors want to ask McVeigh Why?.

text.p: The jurors who sentenced Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh to death have one question for the man convicted of the worst mass murder in U.S. history: Why?

"Why? That's one of the number one questions I would want to ask of him. Why did he do this? Why did he bring this on the heartland of America?" juror David Gilger said in an interview with NBC's "Meet the Press" on Sunday.
The jury of seven men and five women on Friday sentenced McVeigh to death for blowing up the Alfred P. Murrah federal building, killing 168 people in an April 19, 1995, attack that horrified America.
Eleven of the 12 jurors who gave a news conference in Denver on Saturday evening answered with one voice when asked what they would like to ask McVeigh: "Why?"

The explanation offered by both the prosecution and the defence during the seven-week trial -- that McVeigh was enraged by the deaths of 80 Branch Davidian cult members in a 1993 confrontation with federal agents at Waco, Texas -- was not enough for jurors who grappled with the enormity of the crime.
McVeigh was not asked the question because he did not testify.

McVeigh was transferred on Saturday from the cell at the Denver federal courthouse where he had been held during the trial to a federal prison in suburban Denver, local news reports said. Federal Judge Richard Matsch will formally sentence the 29-year-old Gulf War veteran at a later hearing.

McVeigh's lawyers will file appeals that will take several years to wind their way through the courts. Unless the conviction or sentence are overturned, McVeigh could be executed in as early as 2000, legal experts said, a relatively quick time for Death Row appeals.

McVeigh was tried in Denver only for the deaths of eight federal agents killed in the blast. Oklahoma officials have said they may still seek to try him there for the murders of the other 160 people who died.
Terry Nichols, who is accused of helping McVeigh carry out the bombing, will be tried separately later this year.

McVeigh's chief defence attorney Stephen Jones, whose handling of the case has been criticised by some legal experts, was quoted in The Denver Post on Sunday as saying he had mounted a "respectable" defence. "I had to defend the indefensible," he was quoted as saying.
The jurors said they were often overcome with emotion at the suffering of the bombing victims and the gravity of the issues they had to decide.
"Twelve people cried when we pronounced him guilty. It took us a good hour, hour and a half to calm ourselves down so we could go into the courtroom again," juror Ruth Meier said.

The jurors said they needed just one vote to reach a unanimous decision when they found McVeigh guilty on June 2 and when they sentenced him to death last Friday. Before voting, they carefully went through the evidence, concluding it pointed overwhelmingly to McVeigh's guilt.
"The physical evidence was so compelling, so convincing from beginning to end, it became very apparent to me in the final analysis that guilt was the only verdict," jury foreman Jim Osgood said.
Juror John Candelaria said he was "very bothered" that McVeigh showed no emotion. McVeigh sat stiff and expressionless for most of the trial.

Speaking on NBC's "Meet the Press", Christopher Tritico, one of McVeigh's attorneys, said "it would have been wrong" no matter how McVeigh had reacted. "If he'd have cried during the very emotional testimony that we had during this case that would have been seen as an admission of guilt," he said.

Tritico said defence lawyers had decided not to have McVeigh testify during the penalty phase because "if you put him on in a punishment phase, you run a big risk of waiving your appellate issues and we didn't want to run that risk."
He said the defence team would consider several issues as grounds for appeal, including limitations on the jury selection process and Matsch's decision to exclude some evidence.

Matsch prevented the defence from suggesting that an international conspiracy was behind the bombing and from introducing a Department of Justice report critical of the work of the FBI's Washington D.C. crime laboratory in the case.
